ARTICLE: 47.1—All cases of crimes committed by official bondsmen, personal retainers, or government or private slaves,
where the specific article has no formal text concerning these inferior classes,
treat them as commoners.
SUBCOMMENTARY:
Official bondsmen are attached to the Court of Administration of Agriculture.
Prefectures and counties originally did not have their registers of ancestry.
Personal retainers
belong to private households,
and [8a] their wives can be commoners,
female personal retainers,
or slaves.
If the daughter of a personal retainer commits a crime,
it is the same as if committed by an official bondsman or a personal retainer.
If a government or private slave commits a crime
where the specific article has a formal text refers to such crimes

as those against a master or beating commoners.42 42See the discussion on the inferior classes in the fourth part of introduction Chapter II. In cases of petty treason such as a plot to kill their master, execution did not have to wait for a favorable time, but could be carried out as soon as the emperor approved the sentence. Article 321 punishes a master who kills an offending slave by only one hundred blows with the heavy stick. If the slave were blameless, the punishment was only one year of penal servitude.
Each such case follows the specific article.
Where the specific article has no formal text
refers to such crimes as unauthorized entry into the palace, climbing over [such things as customs barriers where a passport is required], crimes against the same class of person,
or cursing one's paternal grandparents, parents, or elder brothers or sisters.
Each such case treats them as commoners.
ARTICLE: Official bondsmen, personal retainers, and slaves who commit crimes punished by life exile or penal servitude
have blows with the heavy stick substituted
and are exempted from forced labor in a fixed place.
SUBCOMMENTARY:
Official bondsmen, personal retainers, and slaves who commit crimes punished by penal servitude
will be treated as specified in the principle of there being no adults in the household save the criminal.43 That is, blows with the heavy stick are substituted. 43Article 27.
For one year of penal servitude
one hundred twenty blows with the heavy stick are substituted—
with an additional twenty blows for each further degree—
to two hundred blows for three years of penal servitude.
They are treated the same for crimes punished by the three degrees of life exile;
the maximum punishment being again two hundred blows with the heavy stick.
After the punishment is administered,
they are returned to the government or their master,
and are exempted from forced labor in a fixed place.
ARTICLE: 47.3a—Official bondsmen, personal retainers, or slaves who must repay the original illicit goods or make redemption by payment of copper and have no goods,
have ten blows with the heavy stick substituted for each two chin of copper.
After the punishment is administered,
they are returned to the government or their master.
SUBCOMMENTARY:
In all cases where a crime has been committed and the original illicit goods must be repaid or redemption by payment of copper made,
and the official bondsmen, personal retainers, or slaves have no goods to make repayment,
the original offense and the original illicit goods are made equivalent to amounts of copper.
Ten blows with the heavy stick are substituted for each two chin of copper,
and after the punishment is administered, the criminals are returned to the government or their master.
Even though the amount of copper required may be more,
the beating may not exceed two hundred [8b] blows.4444Article 29 imposes this limit of two hundred blows with the heavy stick.
Now only original illicit goods have been spoken of,
not doubled illicit goods .45 45In cases of robbery, Article 33 provedes for double repayment of the goods taken.
If the official bondsmen, personal retainers, or slaves have no goods to repay the original illicit goods,
then it is allowed to substitute beating with the heavy stick and release the criminal, exempting him from further punishment.
If they have no goods to repay the doubled illicit goods,
in principle these are not sentenced.
But those who have goods and are able to pay
do so according to the ordinary article.
ARTICLE: 47.3b—Where the official bondsmen, personal retainers, or slaves are aged, young, or disabled,
blows with the heavy stick are not substituted.
Those who have no goods are released and exempted from punishment.
SUBCOMMENTARY:
In the reference above to those who must make repayment or redemption by payment of copper,
if they are seventy years of age or more, fifteen years of age or less, or disabled,

in accordance with this article, blows with the heavy stick are not substituted.46 46The aged and the juvenile had a lesser liability for punishment which is set out in Articles 30 and 31. However, the exemption from beating set forth here is not mentioned though Article 30 does provide that crimes punished by life exile or less may be redeemed.
If upon further investigation they have no goods,
they are released, exempted from punishment, [40] and do not make repayment.
As for cases where personal retainers and slaves must repay illicit goods or make redemption by payment of copper,
this is done by the personal retainers or slaves themselves,
and not by their masters.
ARTICLE: 47.4a—If slaves of the same master should kill each other
and their master request exemption from the death penalty,
it will be reduced one degree.
SUBCOMMENTARY: ARTICLE: 47.4a—
Slaves are an inferior class;
the Code considers them to be domestic animals.
Should they kill one another, even though this should be atoned for by death,
if their master requests exemption from the death penalty,

it will be reduced one degree.4747Article 56 establishes that a reduction of one degree of punishment from either of the two death penalties will be to life exile to 3,000 and that a reduction of one degree from any of the three distances of life exile will be three years of penal servitude.
If a personal retainer intentionally kills a member of the inferior classes belonging to the same master,
this also is punished by death.
But if their master requests exemption from the death penalty,
this same law on reduction of punishment will be permitted.
If a slave killing a slave is a serious crime
and the master's request for exemption from the death penalty is still allowed,
then a personal retainer killing a slave is less serious
and exemption from the death penalty may certainly be allowed
if they belong to the same master.48 48That is, the higher the status of the offender as against that of his victim, the less serious the crime.
This has reference to private ownership.
If the slave belongs to the government,
this article is not applicable.
[9a] COMMENTARY:
47.4b—Should family members kill each other,
the ordinary article is applicable.
SUBCOMMENTARY:
This article states that they are treated as commoners.
Thus it is known that the law for commoners is used.
So for crimes against family members,
this principle on request for exemption and reduction of punishment is not applicable.

ARTICLE: 48.1—49All cases involving foreigners of the same nationality 49There were large numbers of foreigners resident in China during the T'ang period. See the references to them in Schafer, Golden Peaches. A portion of a regulation con­cerning them is found in Article 88. Unlike the fragments discussed in Twitchett, "Tun­huang Fragments of the T'ang Regulations, "p. 373, this regulation quoted in the Code does begin with the word chu 諸, "in all cases." The translation is as follows: "In all cases where a foreigner (fan-jen 蕃人) takes a Chinese woman (Han fu-na 漢婦女) as a wife or concubine, she will not be allowed to return with him to his country."
who have committed crimes against each other
will be sentenced following their own customary law.
48.2—Cases involving those of different nationalities who have committed crimes against each other
will be sentenced following Chinese law.
SUBCOMMENTARY:
Foreigners
refers to persons of those barbarian countries
who have their own rulers and leaders.
They each have their own habits and customs
and their regulations, and the laws are not alike.
In cases involving those of the same nationality who have committed crimes against each other,
the court must ask about the regulations in their native country
and sentence the offense following their customs and laws.
In all cases involving those of different nationalities who have committed crimes against each other,
such as one person from Koryo and another person from Paekche [countries in the Korean peninsula],
Chinese law will be used
to sentence and decide the punishment.
ARTICLE: 49.1—All cases in which a specific article
has a different regulation from that in a principle
follow the specific article.
[9b] SUBCOMMENTARY:
The principle states: "All cases where crimes are committed collectively make the person who formulates the plan the principal.
The accessories have their sentences reduced one degree. ''50 50Article 42.
But the Articles on Assaults and Accusations state: "Where persons plot together to beat or wound someone,
in each case the one who strikes the blow is the main offender and is given the heaviest punishment.
The original plotter's punishment is reduced one degree
and that of the accessories one further degree. ''5151Article 308.
Further, the principle states that
officials of the ninth rank and above
who commit crimes punished by life exile or less will be allowed redemption by payment of copper.52 52Article 11.
The Articles on Judgment and Prison state: "Ranked officials who serve in a position carrying no official rank or in miscellaneous positions
within their own office or in the area under their supervision and commit crimes punished by the heavy stick or less
have punishment administered in accordance with the relevant article. ''5353Artic1e 498.
Cases such as this,
where the specific article is not the same as the principle,
are sentenced according to the specific article.
ARTICLE: 49.2—However, where more than one article may be appropriate,
whichever has the heaviest punishment will be followed.
SUBCOMMENTARY:
According to the Articles on Fraud and Counterfeits,
fraudulent avoidance of taxes and labor services
is punished by two years of penal servitude.54 54Artic1e 380.
But where several adults have been exempted from taxes and labor services,
the law on omitting persons in the Articles on Household and Marriage
punishes omission of one person by one year of penal servitude,
increasing one degree for each further two persons,
and with a maximum [41] punishment of three years of penal servitude.5555Article 150.
also
The Articles on Fraud and Counterfeit also state: "Fraudulent addition of years of merit or subtraction of years of demerit
... which result in office being obtained
is punished by one year of penal servitude. ''56 56Article 370.
But where profit is fraudulently obtained
and there is a large amount of illicit goods,
following the article on obtaining goods and articles by defrauding or cheating the government or private persons.57 57Article 373.
the sentence is comparable to robbery
The maximum punishment is life exile to 3,000 li.5858Article 53 limits the amount of punishment for crimes sentenced as comparable to other crimes to life exile to 3,000 li.
ARTICLE: 49.3a—Cases that are basically more serious but in which the circumstances are not known at the time the crime is committed
are sentenced following the ordinary law.
49.3b—However, those cases that are basically less serious
are sentenced according to the basic circumstances.
SUBCOMMENTARY:
Suppose a paternal uncle and his nephew in the male line
have grown up in different places
and are not known to each other.
Should the nephew hit his paternal uncle and wound him
and the relationship only become known when they are questioned by the officials,

[10a] sentencing will follow the law on assault of persons of non-kin status.5959The difference in punishment is considerable. Hitting and wounding a paternal uncle is punished by life exile to 1,000 li, while the same crime against someone of non-kin status is punished by only sixty blows with the heavy stick. The relevant articles are 328 and 302.
but at another place [so that the robber is not aware of their purpose]
Further, cases such as stealing the objects for the great sacrifices to the spirits,

if the circumstances are not known at the time the crime is committed.6060Here again the punishments differ. Stealing any object belonging to the great spirits was punished by life exile to 2,000 li. However, the punishment for robbery depended upon the value of the goods stolen rather than their status. See Articles 270 and 282.
will all be prosecuted as ordinary theft
As for those cases that are basically less serious,
should a father not recognize his son
or a master his slave
and beat and hit him,
only learning the circumstances afterward,
all such cases follow the relevant laws on hitting sons and slaves
and are not sentenced for assaulting persons of non-kin status... .
ARTICLE: 50.1—All cases involving sentencing of crimes that have no formal article
if the punishment should be decreased.
bring up a heavier offense in order to make clear a lighter punishment (chü-chung yi ming-ch'ing 擧重以明輕)
SUBCOMMENTARY:
Sentencing of crimes that have no formal article
refers to an article
not listing the crime that has been committed.
As for the punishment should be decreased,
according to the Articles on Violence and Robbery:
"[All] cases involving those who enter other people's houses at night without cause [are punished by forty blows with the light stick].
If the master of the house should immediately kill the intruder,
he will not be punished. ''61 61Article 261.
for breaking a limb or wounding.
Thus it is clear that there will be no prosecution
Further,
for such crimes as robbery of goods from relatives of the fifth or closer degree of mourning,

according to the degree of relationship the punishment is reduced below that for the same crime against persons of non-kin status.62 62Article 287. For fifth-degree mourning relatives, the punishment would be reduced one degree below that for ordinary robbery; for third-degree mourning relatives, the reduction would be two degrees; and three degrees for second-degree mourning rela­tives.
For crimes such as fraud or cheating, or illicit goods obtained through malfeasance, and the like,
even though the article has no text on reduction of punishment,
punishment will still be reduced.
Thus it is clear that other crimes follow this article on reduction of punishment.
For them, a heavier offense is brought up to make clear a lighter punishment.
ARTICLE: 50.2—If the punishment should be increased,
then a lighteroffense is brought up to make clear a heavier punishment.
[10b] SUBCOMMENTARY:
It is submitted that the Articles on Violence and Robbery state:
"Those who plot to kill a relative of a higher generation, or of the same generation but older than themselves within the second degree of mourning
... will all be decapitated. ''63 63Article 253.
The text is not concerned with their being either already wounded or killed.
Thus if they are either killed or wounded,
the lighter offense of plotting is brought up
as still calling for the death penalty.
If someone has been killed or there is a plot and someone has already been wounded, this should be punished more heavily then,
and it is clear that they all should be decapitated.
Further, the principle states:

"For cases involving the beating or accusing to the court of one's relatives in the third degree of mourning, whether of a higher generation, or of the same generation but older than oneself, or of a relative in the fourth degree of mourning of an older generation than oneself,
the clause on protection may not be used. ''64 64Article 15.
Thus if a relative of a higher generation, or of the same generation but older than the offender within the one year degree of mourning should be beaten or accused to the court,
the case of the third-degree mourning relative is brought up as the lighter offense.
Since the case involving the relative within the second degree of mourning is punished more heavily,
protection also may not be used.
This is bringing up a lighter offense to make clear a heavier punishment.
ARTICLE: 51.1—All references to the emperor or to the imperial cortege
include his paternal grandmother, his mother, and his empress, and their corteges as well.
SUBCOMMENTARY:
In regard to the emperor,
it is submitted that the Articles on Violence and Robbery state:
"Robbery of the emperor's possessions or goods
is punished by life exile to 2,500 li.''65 65Article 270; Deloustal 429.
Robbery of the possessions or goods of his paternal grandmother, his mother, and his empress
receives [42] the same punishment.
With regard to the imperial cortege,
according to the Articles on the Imperial Guard and Prohibitions:
(the imperial cortege)
"Interference with the imperial cortege is punished by one year of penal servitude. ''66 66Article 74.
Interference with the cortege of any of the three empresses
is also punished by one year of penal servitude.
A further example:
to enter the imperial presence without authorization
is punished by decapitation.67 67Article 59; Deloustal 51.
To enter the presence of any of the three empresses
is also punished by decapitation.
This means that the offenses are considered to be the same.
ARTICLE: 51.2—In reference to imperial decrees and edicts,

the punishment for violation of orders of the emperor's paternal grandmother, his mother, his empress, and the crown prince is reduced one degree below the punishment for violating imperial decrees and edicts.
[11a] SUBCOMMENTARY:
According to the Statutes on Public Standards:
"The three empresses and the crown prince issue orders. ''6868Niida, Statutes, p. 548.
The Administrative Regulations state:
"Cases of violation of imperial decrees that have been issued
are punished by two years of penal servitude. ''69 69Article 112; Deloustal 119.
However, the punishment for violation of the orders of the three empresses and the crown prince
is reduced one degree.
(either because of a crime or error within the palace of the crown prince, or because of some violation by the palace guard)

ARTICLE: 51.3a—Cases that require prosecution either because of a crime or error within the palace of the crown prince, or because of some violation by the palace guard are also considered the same as under this principle on reduction of punishment.
SUBCOMMENTARY:
Cases of crimes against the crown prince

refer to criticizing the crown prince or resisting or driving away messengers carrying the orders of the crown prince,70 70Article 132 punishes criticism of the emperor with decapitation. The other offenses mentioned below are punished varyingly.
the accessories of chariots and horses not matching, or the equipment not being in order,
as well as entering the palace of the crown prince without authorization,
or guards who stand night duty falsifying their names and replacing each other, or guards who put down their arms, suddenly leave their duties and sleep in another place;
such are called crimes.
Mistakes
refer to such cases as failure to follow the correct prescription when preparing medicine for the crown prince, or making a mistake in attaching the label,
as well as guards not being aware that someone has entered the palace of the crown prince without authorization.
The sentences for both crimes and mistakes
are reduced one degree below sentences for the same crimes and mistakes involving the emperor.
COMMENTARY:
51.3b—However, cases that basically come within the ten abominations
even though there is a reduction of punishment.
follow the relevant law
SUBCOMMENTARY:
This refers to crimes and mistakes affecting the crown prince
being comparable to and included in the laws affecting the emperor. Thus crimes that come within the ten abominations
even though there is a reduction of punishment.
[11b] follow the relevant laws
ARTICLE: 52.1—All references to relatives of the second degree of mourning and to paternal grandparents
include paternal great- and great-great-grandparents as well.
SUBCOMMENTARY:
As for references to relatives of the second degree of mourning,
the Articles on the Household and Marriage state:
"Those who marry during the period of mourning for a relative of the second degree of mourning
are punished by one hundred blows with the heavy stick. ''71 71Article 179.
Thus marriage during the period of mourning for paternal great- and great-great-grandparents
is considered the same as during the period of mourning for a relative of the second degree of mourning.
As for paternal grandparents,
the Articles on the Household and Marriage state:
"While the paternal grandparents or parents are still living,
to have a separate household register or separate goods
is punished by three years of penal servitude. ''72 72Article 155. This crime also comes under the ten abominations.
while the paternal great- or great-great-grandparents
Thus, the punishment for having a separate household register or separate goods
are still living is considered to be the same.
Therefore, it is stated that references to relatives of the second degree of mourning and to paternal grandparents
include paternal great-
and great-great-grandparents as well.
ARTICLE: 52.2—References to grandsons in the male line
include great-and great-great-grandsons in the male line as well.
[43] SUBCOMMENTARY:
The Articles on Assaults and Accusations state:
"Sons and grandsons in the male line who violate teachings and commands
... are punished by two years of penal servitude. ''73 73Article 348.
Thus great-and
great-great-grandsons in the male line who violate teachings and commands
are also punished by two years of penal servitude... .
ARTICLE: 52.3a—If a grandson in the male line by the proper wife be comes the heir of his paternal grandparents,
they are considered to be the same as his father and mother.
SUBCOMMENTARY:
According to ritual and the statute:
"If there is no son by the proper wife,
then a grandson of the proper wife is made heir. ''74 74Niida, Statutes, pp. 305-306.
Thus the grandson in the male line becomes the heir of his paternal grandparents.
If hearing of the death of his paternal grandparents
[12a] he conceals and does not mourn their death,
the punishment is life exile to 2,000 li.75 75Article 120.
Therefore it is stated that they are considered to be the same as his father and mother.
COMMENTARY:
52.3b—Cases of collective prosecution
each follow this basic law concerning paternal grandparents and grandsons in the male line.
SUBCOMMENTARY:
According to the Articles on Violence and Robbery,
in cases of rebellion and sedition
the father and sons of the criminal who are sixteen years of age and over are all punished by strangulation.
His paternal grandfather and grandsons in the male line are enslaved by the state.76 76Article 248; Deloustal 410.
But if a grandson in the male line of the proper wife has become the heir of his grandparents,
he is enslaved and not killed.
Therefore, it is stated that each case follows this basic law concerning paternal grand­parents and grandsons in the male line.
ARTICLE: 52.4—The proper mother, stepmother, and foster mother
as well as adopted parents
are considered to be the same as parents.
SUBCOMMENTARY:
... As for foster mother,
according to ritual,
if a concubine has no children,
or a concubine's children have no mother
and the father orders them to be mother and child,
this relationship is that of foster mother.
If the father had not ordered it,
according to ritual, the relationship would be that of the fourth degree of mourning
and not that of mother.
Adopted parents
refers to cases where there are no children
and a son is adopted from the same clan.
Foster mothers and others
are all referred to as mother,
but adopted parents
also include the father... .
ARTICLE: 52.5a—References to children
include both male and female.
SUBCOMMENTARY:
As for references to children,
the Articles on Violence and Robbery state:
"Sons and grandsons in the male line who violate teachings and commands
... are punished by two years of penal servitude.'"
Here both male and female are included.
[12b] Cases of collective prosecution
refer to such crimes as killing three members of one family.
Collective prosecution extends to wives and sons,
but daughters are exempted from punishment.
Therefore it is stated that females are not included.
However, collective prosecution does extend to females in the specific articles on rebellion, sedition, or the making or keeping of ku poison.
Where the specific articles include females in collective prosecution,
the relevant law is followed.
ARTICLE: 52.6—In cases that refer to relatives of the sixth degree of mourning or closer,
the sentence is according to the original mourning relationship,
which may not be lowered because of higher position or reduced by marriage or adoption.
Mourning relationship due to affection is considered to be the same as formal mourning relationship.
SUBCOMMENTARY:
The emperor's protection extends to his relatives of the sixth or closer degree of mourning.
According to the Articles on the Household and Marriage:
"Marriage to the former wife of a relative of the sixth degree of mourning

is punished by one hundred blows of the heavy stick for both. ''7878Article 183. Marriage between relatives was forbidden in traditional China. In the case of fifth-degree mourning relatives, Article 411 punishes both partners to the marriage by three years of penal servitude. Even persons of the same surname who married were punished by two years of penal servitude. See Article 182.
If the imperial house severs mourning relations with a collateral relative of the second degree of mourning, or a woman is married,
or a man is adopted outside the family,
all of these actions lower the mourning relationship by one degree.
But if there is a crime and protection is sought,
each case is according to the original mourning relationship,
which may not be lowered because of higher position or reduced by marriage or adoption. Thus the law regarding the lesser mourning relationships is followed.
Mourning relationships due [44] to affection
are those such as that of the wife and concubine for the husband,
the concubine for the husband's eldest son, and the wife for her parents-in-law.
If such persons commit offenses against each other, the crimes are considered to be the same as for formal mourning relationships.
ARTICLE: 53.1a—All references to reciprocal punishment, both with regard to punishment and sentence, are for the same punishment that the victim would have suffered,
and the sentence is limited to that punishment.
SUBCOMMENTARY:
As for references to reciprocal punishment,
the Articles on Assaults and Accusations state:
"Those who falsely accuse other persons
are reciprocally punished."79 79Article 342. See the discussion in the second part of introduction Chapter II.
As for punishment,
[13a] the principle states:
"If the confession is untruthful or incomplete,
crimes that have not been confessed truthfully or completely will be punished. ''8080Article 37.
As for sentence,
according to the principle:
"In cases of other illicit goods where prosecution is required,
if the criminal repents his fault and returns them to the owner,
his sentence will be reduced three degrees below the original punishment. ''8181Article 39.
As for the same punishment,
the Articles on Fraud and Counterfeits state:
"If a translator either through fraud or counterfeit
causes an offense to have the punishment either decreased or increased,
he is given the same punishment. ''8282Article 387.
As for sentence is limited to that crime,
this means that from reciprocal punishment on down in this article,
that sentence is limited to that punishment.
These offenses are not the same as actual crimes.
Therefore the death penalty is limited to strangulation.
ARTICLE: 53.2—References to cases sentenced as comparable to taking bribes and subverting the law, comparable to robbery, and the like,
mean that the punishment is limited to life exile to 3,000 li
but is otherwise comparable.
SUBCOMMENTARY:
As for references to sentences as comparable to taking bribes and subverting the law,
the Articles on Administrative Regulations state:
"If bribes are not accepted at first,
but are taken after the crime,
and the law has been subverted
in sentencing the crime, the case is sentenced as comparable to subverting the law. ''84 84Article 139.
Another article states that
forcing the market or gaining excessive profits within an official's area of supervision
(gaining excessive profits)
is sentenced as comparable to subverting the law.8585Article 142. See also the discussion in translation Chapter IV, note 55.
As for references to sentences as comparable to robbery, and the like,
the Articles on Fraud and Counterfeits state:
"Taking goods and articles by fraud or cheating, whether from the government or private persons,
is sentenced as comparable to robbery. ''86 86Article 373.
The Miscellaneous Articles state:
"The throwing away or destruction of tallies or ensigns or gate keys
is sentenced as comparable to robbery. ''87 87Article 437.
Crimes such as these,
which are sentenced as comparable to subverting the law or comparable to robbery,
limit the punishment to life exile to 3,000 li.
Thus, cases involving comparable punishment
limit the punishment.
They are not the same as actual crimes.

ARTICLE: 53.3—None of these crimes comes within the principles on disenrollment, resignation from office, double repayment of illicit goods, added punishment for crimes committed by supervisory or custodial officials, or life exile with added labor.
[13b] SUBCOMMENTARY:...
Even though the relevant laws do not call for reduction of punishment,
these crimes are considered the same as under the laws on miscellaneous crimes, and the sentence is reduced.8888That is, Article 11 is applicable.
ARTICLE: 53.4—Reference to cases sentenced for subverting the law, for robbery, and the like,
mean that the punishment is the same as for the actual crime.
SUBCOMMENTARY:
As for sentenced for subverting the law,
the Articles on the Family and Marriage state:

"If the village headman or official in charge fraudulently omit households, leave out individuals, or add to or subtract from persons' ages in order to decrease or increase the amounts of taxes and labor services
... and a large amount of illicit goods comes to themselves,
the case is sentenced as subverting the law. ''89 89Article 153.
Another article states:
"If taxes are collected [45] illegally or arbitrarily .. . going into private hands,
the case is sentenced as subverting the law. ''9090Article 173.
As for cases sentenced for robbery and the like,
the Articles on Violence and Robbery state that
where government property is exchanged,
the part that is calculated to be profit
is sentenced as robbery.91 91Article 290.
The Articles on the Public Stables and Granaries state:
"In cases of supervisory or custodial officials who make unauthorized personal use of government property
or lend it to other persons
without a written record,
both the officials and those who borrow it are sentenced for robbery.' 9292Article 212.
Where the crime is considered to be the same as actual subversion of the law or actual robbery,
disenrollment or resignation from office, and double repayment of illicit goods all follow as if for a normal crime.
Cases of intentionalkilling or wounding, killing or wounding by assault, or illicit sexual intercourse, and so on,
are sentenced the same as actual crimes. . .
ARTICLE: 54.1—All references to supervisory officials mean that
those who are in charge of offices or who investigate cases are supervisory officials.
SUBCOMMENTARY:
In charge of
refers to all offices both in the capital and in the provinces whose senior officers are in charge of the areas under their control.
Investigate cases
refers to the executive officials in offices who decide cases and sentence crimes.
COMMENTARY:
in prefectures, counties, garrisons, frontier posts, intrepid militia,93 and so on, 930n the intrepid militia, see des Rotours, Fonctionnaires, II, 548 ff.
Those who are executive officers or above
are all supervisory officials.

(executive officials and above in prefectures, counties, garrisons, frontier posts, intrepid militia, and so on)
This means that even though the positions and duties of executive officials and above in prefectures, counties, garrisons, frontier posts, intrepid militia, and so on, are not the same,
nevertheless, within the area under their control they all are considered to be supervisory officials under this principle.
Officers in garrisons, frontier posts, and intrepid militia
are only in charge of soldiers
and not their family members.
COMMENTARY: Officers in
As for other offices,
as long as an official is in charge of an office or an investigation,
even if he is only in charge of individuals and not their family members,
if he commits illicit sexual intercourse or takes goods, such cases also come within this principle on surveillance.
[14b] SUBCOMMENTARY:
Other offices
refers to offices other than prefectures, counties, garrisons, frontier posts, and intrepid militia
all having supervisory officials.
whether in a department, a tribunal, a court, a directory, a guard office,
or any other office is a supervisory official.
Whoever is appointed
to be even nominally in charge of an office,
If he then investigates matters,
this is a supervisory function.
Even though the Department of State governs the prefectures and superior prefectures,
if there are no documents involved,
this is not ordinarily a supervisory function.
All offices, both in the capital and in the provinces, follow this principle.
if an officer is in command of soldiers and scribes but not their family members
this also comes within this principle on supervision.
As for the imperial guards,
and he commits illicit sexual intercourse with one of their family members or takes goods from their households,
An officer of intrepid militia only commands his militiamen,
and if he commits illicit sexual intercourse with one of their family members or takes goods from their households,
both of these offenses come within this law on supervision.96 96The effect is to increase the punishment. Article 18 also requires resignation from office.
Offices both within the capital and in the provinces,
where an official has illicit sexual intercourse or takes goods from households that are not under his control, all follow this principle.
[46] QUERY:
If a junior officer
robs the households of the guards under his command of goods,
is this the same as a supervisory official taking goods or not?

under his command.
A junior officer has only guards
and since the goods were not taken [by coercion, or as a bribe],
Robbery is not covered under this article

[15a] ARTICLE: 54.2—References to custodial officials
take those whose duties are personal protection to be custodial officials.
even though their regular duties are neither supervisory nor custodial.
54.3—Those who temporarily serve as supervisory or custodial officials are considered as such,
SUBCOMMENTARY:
Custodial
refers to those who issue decisions to clerks
and have sole control over matters, as well as those who supervise granaries, jails, miscellaneous articles, and the like.
Those whose regular duties are neither supervisory nor custodial
even though they are officials whose regular duties are neither to govern nor to direct.
refers to those who are sent temporarily to serve as supervisory or custodial officials
being considered as such,
ARTICLE: 55.1—All references to day
take it to be one hundred k'o 刻. But
is used in calculating labor.
But dawn to dusk
SUBCOMMENTARY:
The Articles on Administrative Regulations state:
"Officials who, without a reason, do not take their turn at duty
are beaten twenty blows with the light stick for each day. ''97 97Article 95.
Here the basis for prosecution is a whole day and night, one hundred k'o.
As for calculating labor,
the Articles on Administrative Regulations state:
"Supervisory officials
who make unauthorized use of labor within their area of supervision
... in each case have the labor calculated and are sentenced for taking goods and articles within their area of supervision. "98 98Article 143.
Here dawn to dusk
is a day.
It is not necessary to take one hundred k'o as a standard.
COMMENTARY:
If there has been much use of labor,
even though not a full day,

[15b] SUBCOMMENTARY:
As for calculating much use of labor,
if two men work
from dawn to noon,
this is one day's labor.
If six men each work
for two hours,
this is also one day's labor.
No matter whether many men each work for a segment of time
or one man works many days,
segments of time are used to count the total.
ARTICLE: 55.2—References to year
consider it to be three hundred sixty days.
SUBCOMMENTARY:
In the Code there is much reference to "year''
as a basis for penal servitude and labor.
Years are calculated by days;
references to year do not consider it to be twelve months.
ARTICLE: 55.3—References to persons' ages
take the household register as a standard.
SUBCOMMENTARY:
References to persons' ages
then must take the household register as a standard.
Some persons' appearance is that of great age while they are young,
others appear young when their age is great.
All cases follow the household register
and not appearance.
The household register is compiled once each three years.
If the year is not one in which the household register is compiled,
then the person's age is calculated from the old household register.
[47] QUERY:
The Household Statutes state:
"If there is doubt in regard to abuses or deceit,
the appearance of those involved is taken as a standard. "99 99Niida, Statutes, pp. 242-243.
If a crime is committed and the age and appearance of the accused are greatly different,
is the statute's taking appearance as a standard followed in sentencing the crime or not?
REPLY:
The Statutes' text concerns100 taxes and labor services, 100Yî 以 should be read wei 爲, following the SPTK edition.
while that of the Code determines punishment and sets up regulations.
(gain mitigation of punishment)
If a person's appearance could gain mitigation of punishment then abuses would flourish.
[16a] Taxes and labor services are less serious,
therefore appearance may temporarily be taken as a standard.
But matters concerning punishment are serious,
and may only follow the household register.
If the meanings of the Code
and the Statutes are different,
that of the Code may not be rejected and that of the Statutes followed.
If someone who has the appearance of an adult commits a capital crime
and the household register gives his age as seven years,
he may not be sentenced.101 101See Article 30.
Or if someone whom the household register lists as being sixteen102 years of age or above commits a capital crime 102Liu-shih 六十 should read shih-liu 十六, following the SPTK edition.
and upon investigation he has the appearance
of not being over seven years of age,
in matters such as this,
where the appearance and the age given by the household register are greatly at variance,
if the crime is punished by life exile or more, or involves disenrollment, resignation from office, or the use of office to replace punishment,
a memorial is sent up to the Department of State for consideration and decision.
Where the throne must be memorialized,
a provisional memorial is sent up to get the emperor's decision.
ARTICLE: 55.4—References to groups (chung 衆)
mean three or more persons.
55.5—References to plots
mean two or more persons.
SUBCOMMENTARY:
As for references to groups,
the Articles on Judgment and Prison state that
officials of the seventh rank and above

who commit crimes may not be tortured [to gain a confession].103 103Article 474. The same rights are given those seventy years of age or more, or fifteen years of age or less, as well as the disabled.
Rather, conviction depends upon evidence given by a group.
The group must be three persons or more; only then can it be considered a group.
Other references to groups
also follow this text.
As for plots,
the Articles on Violence and Robbery state:
"Those who plot to kill people are punished by three years of penal servitude. ''104 104Article 256.
However, the plot must have two or more persons.
References to plots in other articles
all follow this principle.
COMMENTARY:
If the circumstances of the plot are clear and evident,
then one person may be considered to be the same as two persons.105105The same is true in plotting rebellion. See Article 248; Deloustal 410.
SUBCOMMENTARY:
If someone enters another person's home carrying a knife or club,
and investigation proves them to be enemies
who each desire to kill the other,
then even though there be only one person,
this situation is considered the same as a plot.
Therefore it is stated that one person may be considered the same as two persons.
ARTICLE: 56.1—All references to addition
mean a degree of increase.
56.2a—All references to reduction
mean a degree of decrease.
SUBCOMMENTARY:
If someone commits a crime punished by one hundred blows with the heavy stick
[and some other circumstance] adds one degree of punishment,
then the sentence is to one year of penal servitude.106 106Such a circumstance might be that a slave hit a commoner.
a required year of penal servitude,
If one degree of punishment is added to
the sentence is to one and one-half years of penal servitude.
This is called a degree of increase.
Further, if a crime is punished by one year of penal servitude
[and some other circumstance] requires that the punishment be reduced one degree,
then the sentence is to one hundred blows with the heavy stick.107 107Here the circumstance might be that a commoner hit a slave.
Or, if one hundred blows with the heavy stick
and a reduction of one degree is required,
then ninety blows with the heavy stick are administered.
This is called a degree of decrease.
ARTICLE: 56.2b—The two death penalties and the three degrees of life exile
are both considered to be one degree of reduction of punishment.
SUBCOMMENTARY:
If a crime is committed that is punished by decapitation
and the accessories have their punishment reduced one degree,
then the sentence is to life exile to 3,000 li.108 108Accessories usually have their punishment reduced one degree below that of the principals. See Article 42.
Or if a crime is committed that is punished by life exile to 3,000 li,
and some principle calls for reduction of one degree,
then the sentence is to three years of penal servitude.
Therefore, it is stated that the two death penalties and the three degrees of life exile
are both considered to be one degree of reduction of punishment.
Where reduction of punishment is required for life exile with added labor,
it is considered the same as under this law on the three degrees of life exile.
[48] ARTICLE: 56.3a—In adding,
the number must be complete to be prosecuted.
56.3b—Further, adding to punishment may not extend to the death penalty.
But where the specific article adds punishment extending to the death penalty,
the specific article is followed.
[17a] SUBCOMMENTARY:
In adding, the number must be complete to be prosecuted.
Suppose someone commits a robbery of goods
lacking only one ts'un of being worth ten p'i of silk.
According to the Articles on Violence and Robbery,
robbery by stealth of goods worth five p'i of silk is punished by one year of penal servitude.
One degree of punishment is added for each additional five p'i.109 109Article 282.
But since one ts'un was lacking,
the punishment is only one year of penal servitude.
Further, adding punishment may not extend to the death penalty.
According to the Articles on Arrests and Taking Flight:
"If a guard is on duty and takes flight,
the punishment is one hundred blows with the heavy stick for the first day,
with one degree of punishment added for each further two days. ''110 110Article 460.
Even though the text gives no maximum punishment,
this is limited to life exile to 3,000 li
and may not extend to the death penalty.
But where the specific article adds punishment extending to the death penalty, the specific article is followed.
The Articles on Assaults and Accusations state that
for beating a person so as to break two limbs,
the punishment is life exile to 3,000 li.111 111Article 305.
Another article states that
if a personal retainer beats and wounds a commoner,
one degree of punishment is added beyond that for the same crime committed by a commoner.112 112Article 320.
adding punishment
may extend to the death penalty.
Thus in a specific article,
COMMENTARY:
56.3c—Adding punishment may extend to strangulation
but not to decapitation.
SUBCOMMENTARY:
If a personal retainer strikes a commoner
and breaks two limbs,
the punishment is already strangulation.
If the beating and breaking of limbs is deliberate,
another degree of punishment is added.
Here, however, additional punishment may only extend to strangulation,
it may not extend further to decapitation.
ARTICLE: 56.4a—Where punishment is only one-half year of penal servitude
and it is required to substitute blows with the heavy stick,
the number is one hundred.
56.4b—If a reduction of punishment is required,
ninety blows with the heavy stick is the next amount.
[17b] SUBCOMMENTARY:
If a county clerk
deliberately increases the circumstances affecting a prisoner
so that one-half year of penal servitude is added,
and the deputy magistrate knows of this and sentences an increase of punishment,
then the clerk is the principal
and is punished by one-half year of penal servitude.
Should the clerk be the single adult member of his household,
then one hundred blows with the heavy stick are administered.
The deputy magistrate's punishment is required to be reduced one degree,
so that he is sentenced to ninety blows with the heavy stick
or payment of nine chin of copper.
ARTICLE: 57.1—All references to Taoist priests and nuns
include Buddhist priests and nuns as well.
SUBCOMMENTARY:
The Miscellaneous Articles state that
cases of illicit sexual intercourse by Taoist priests and nuns
have two degrees of punishment added beyond that for commoners.113 113Article 416.
In other articles, references to Taoist priests and nuns
include Buddhist priests and nuns as well.
In all cases where the crime of illicit sexual intercourse is committed at the time that one is a Taoist priest or nun
and the crime is discovered after return to lay status,
punishment is still added in accordance with the time that the crime was committed.
However, they are considered the same as commoners in that if sent into penal servitude

they may not use their certificate of ordination (kao-tieh 告牒) to replace the punishment.114114A photograph of a provisional certificate of ordination for a monk is given at the back of Jacques Gernet, Les Aspects économiques du bouddhisme.
ARTICLE: 57.2a—The relationship of Taoist and Buddhist priests and nuns to their masters
is the same as for paternal uncles and aunts.
SUBCOMMENTARY:
Masters
in Taoist and Buddhist monasteries.
refer to those who expound canonical texts and teachings
Such persons are teaching masters.
Crimes against them
are punished the same as against paternal uncles and aunts.
According to the Articles on Assaults and Accusations,
cursing paternal uncles or aunts
is punished by one year of penal servitude.115 115Article 329.
Cursing a teaching master
is also punished by one year of penal servitude.
Crimes against the teaching master in other articles
all consider him to be of the same relationship as a paternal uncle or aunt.
[18a; 49] ARTICLE: 57.2b—The master's relationship to his disciples
is the same as for nephews and nieces in the male line.
SUBCOMMENTARY:
This refers to what has been explained in the text above.
Crimes committed by a teaching master against his disciples
are considered the same as those by a laymen against his nephews and nieces in the male line.
According to the Articles on Assaults and Accusations,
beating and killing nephews and nieces in the male line
is punished by three years of penal servitude.116116Article 328.
The Articles on Violence and Robbery state that
cases ofintentionally killing relatives of the second degree of mourning or less, whether of a lower generation, or of the same generation but younger than oneself, because of greed,
is punished by strangulation.117 117Article 287.
Nephews and nieces in the male line are relatives of the second degree of mourning of a lower generation, or of the same generation but younger than oneself.
Should a teaching master beat and kill a disciple because of anger,
the punishment is three years of penal servitude.
Cases of deliberate killing because of greed
are sentenced to strangulation.
ARTICLE: 57.3a—The relationship of the Taoist or Buddhist monastery's personal retainers and slaves to the three authorities
is the same as to a master's relatives of the second degree of mourning.
SUBCOMMENTARY:
Taoist monasteries have abbots, chief administrators, and masters of ceremonies.
Buddhist monasteries have abbots, chief administrators, and directors of prayers.
These are the three authorities.
Should a personal retainer or slave
commit a crime against one of the three authorities in their monastery,
it is the same as that of a personal retainer or slave against his master's relatives of the second degree of mourning.
According to the Articles on Assaults and Accusations,
if a master beats and kills a personal retainer,
the punishment is one year of penal servitude.118 118Article 322.
In another article,
if a slave commits a crime
and his master kills him without having asked the court's permission,
the punishment is one hundred blows with the heavy stick.119 119Article 321.
The commentary states:
"If the master's relatives of the one year degree of mourning .. . kill the slave,
it is considered the same as the master's doing it.
Articles below on personal retainers follow this law.''
Another article states that
personal retainers or slaves who beat their master 's relatives of the second degree of mourning
are punished by strangulation.
If they curse them,
the punishment is two years of penal servitude.120120Article 323.
If the three authorities beat and kill their monastery's personal retainers,
this is punished by one year of penal servitude.
If a slave commits a crime
and they kill him without having asked the court's permission,
the punishment is one hundred blows with the heavy stick.
If a [18b] personal retainer or slave beats one of the three authorities,
the punishment is strangulation.
If he curses one of them,
the punishment is two years of penal servitude.
ARTICLE: 57.3b—The relationship of the monastery's personal retainers and slaves to the other priests
is the same as to a master's relatives of the fifth degree of mourning.
SUBCOMMENTARY:
The Articles on Assaults and Accusations state:
"A personal retainer or slave who beats his master's relatives of the fifth degree of mourning
is punished by one year of penal servitude.
If the wound is serious,
one degree of punishment is added beyond that for the same crime committed by a commoner. ''121121Ibid.
Another article states that
if they beat or break a limb, or wound or offend even more seriously against a personal retainer or slave of one of their master's relatives of the fifth degree of mourning,
(break a limb, or wound or offend even more seriously)
the punishment for each of these offenses is reduced two degrees below that for killing or wounding a personal retainer or slave of someone who is not kin to their master.122122Article 324.
Another article states:
"If they beat, wound, or kill another person's personal retainers,
the punishment is reduced one degree below that for killing a commoner.
If the victim is a slave,
the reduction of punishment is two degrees. ''123123Article 320.
Thus, if a personal retainer
beats a Taoist or Buddhist priest or nun of the same monastery,
each such offense is punished by one year of penal servitude.
If the wound is serious,
each such offense has one degree of punishment added beyond that for the same offense against a commoner.
If the personal retainer beats a Taoist or Buddhist priest or another of those persons named above and breaks a tooth,
the punishment is two years of penal servitude.
If the offense is by a slave,
another degree of punishment is added,
the penalty being two and one-half years of penal servitude... .
COMMENTARY:
Cases of illicit sexual intercourse and robbery
are considered the same as against persons of non-kin status.
SUBCOMMENTARY:
If Taoist or Buddhist priests or nuns commit illicit sexual intercourse or robbery,
the law regards these crimes as being extremely serious.
Therefore, even though they are committed against personal retainers or slaves of the same monastery,
they are considered the same as if against commoners.
This means that if the three authorities or lower officials commit illicit sexual intercourse [50] or robbery,
the punishment is not different from that for these crimes committed against commoners.
If their slaves [19a] commit illicit sexual intercourse or robbery,
the punishment is the same as if committed against a person of non-kin status.
If a disciple robs his teaching master or a teaching master his disciples,
this also is treated the same as under the law on robbery of persons of non-kin status.
If goods are held in common
and a disciple takes them for his own use,
this is considered the same as if someone of a lower generation, or of the same generation but younger than others who dwell together appropriated goods for his own use.124 124Article 162.
For goods worth ten p 'i of silk, the punishment is ten blows with the light stick,
with one degree of punishment added for each further ten p'i of silk.
The maximum punishment is one hundred blows with the heavy stick.
But if the goods are not worth ten p'i of silk,
there is no prosecution.125125Article 56.
[1a; 2.50] CHAPTER VII
SUBCOMMENTARY: The Articles on the Imperial Guard and Prohibitions
were not in the codes of the Ch'in, Han, and Wei dynasties.
Chia Ch'ung, the prime minister of the Chin dynasty, and others,
consulted the codes of the Han and Wei dynasties
and, according to the circumstances, added to and subtracted from them,
making this section
and calling it the Articles on the Imperial Palace and the Imperial Guard.1 1See Vol. I, p. 52, and Balazs, Traité juridique, pp. 206 ff.
from the Sung dynasty down through the Latter Chou dynasty.
This name was not changed
Coming to the Northern Ch'i dynasty,
a section on customs barrier gate prohibitions was appended to the Articles on the Imperial Palace and the Imperial Guard
and the name was changed to the Articles on Prohibitions and the Imperial Guard.
During the K'ai -huang period of the Sui dynasty, the name was changed to the Articles on the Imperial Guard and Prohibitions.
The imperial guard
refers to the laws on the jurisdiction of the imperial guard,
whereas prohibitions
takes its name from the prohibitions regarding customs barriers.
Because of veneration of the emperor, to warn against doing what is wrong,
and because the offenses described in this section are especially serious,
it is placed next to the General Principles section,
at the head of all the other sections.
ARTICLE: 58.1a—All cases of unauthorized entry (lan-ju 闌入) of the gates of the imperial ancestral temple, the imperial tombs, or the gates of the imperial grave area
are punished by two years of penal servitude.22 The character men 門 indicates both gates and doors in Chinese. I have used either English word as it best seems to fit the context.
SUBCOMMENTARY:
T'ai 太 "great"
means ta 大 "large."
Miao 廟 "temple"
refers to mao 貌 "delineating the ancestors." 3 3This is an example of definition by homophone. See Vol. I, p. 55, n. 46.
Because the spirits of the ancestors dwell inside them,
such places are called imperial ancestral temples.
As for tombs (shan-ling 山陵),
the San-ch'in chi states that
the Ch'in dynasty called the emperor's tomb a mountain (shan),
while the Han dynasty called it a tumulus (ling). 4 4 The San-ch'in chi 三秦記 was written by one Hsin Mou 辛某 whose dates are not known. This is a paraphrase.
These two terms are also combined
to indicate that the tombs are [lb] high and large like mountains and tumuli.
As for the gates of the imperial grave area,
The Filial Piety Classic states:
"One divines their grave site." 5 5 Hsiao-ching, "Sang ch'in," p. 55; Legge, Hsiao King, p. 487.
If a favorable omen is obtained,
the area of the divination is enclosed and made a grave site.
Imperial guardsmen are stationed at all of these places to protect them,

and those persons who are permitted to go in or out are all listed on a name register.6 .. .6 Name registers (ming-chi 名籍) were commonly used to control entry to places connected with the emperor or the imperial family. See Article 59 immediately below.
entry of the rooms of the imperial ancestral temple,
This article provides no punishment for

but in accordance with the text below, which reduces the punishment for offenses connected with the imperial ancestral temple one degree below those connected with the imperial palace,7 7See Article 79 below.
the punishment should be one degree less than for unauthorized entry into the imperial presence,
or life exile at a distance of 3,000 li.
Climbing onto the tombs without a reason
is punished the same as entry of the rooms of the imperial ancestral8 temple.8Miao 廟 should be inserted before shih 室, following the KHCPTS edition.
ARTICLE: 58.1b—Climbing over a wall
is punished by three years of penal servitude.
58.2—Offenses connected with the Altar of the Soil
are punished one degree less in each case.
58.3a—If the guardsmen are not aware of the offense,
their punishment is reduced two degrees below that of the criminal.
SUBCOMMENTARY:...
Climbing over the wall of the Altar of the Soil or entering without authorization
are both punished one degree less than for the same offense involving the imperial ancestral temple.
Guardsmen
refer to soldiers serving as imperial guardsmen who are standing guard at the imperial ancestral temple, imperial tombs, and the Altar of the Soil.
If they are not aware that someone has climbed over the wall or entered without authorization,
their punishment is reduced one degree below that of the criminal in each case.
Guardsmen
refer to those who take turns standing duty [51] during the day and night.
If they are not standing duty (at the time of the offense) they are not punished.
ARTICLE: 58.3b—If the commanding officer is not aware of the offense, his punishment is reduced one degree further.
SUBCOMMENTARY:
Commanding officers
refer to those in command of imperial guardsmen at the imperial ancestral temple, the imperial tombs, and the Altar of the Soil.
Where the rank is provisional, the officer is still punished,
irrespective of rank.
They also have their punishment reduced one degree further
and are only punished when they are personally in charge.
ARTICLE: 58.3c—Those who deliberately connive at such offenses
receive the same punishment as the criminal.
SUBCOMMENTARY:
Deliberate connivance
refers to knowing that a person should not be allowed to enter and yet allowing that person to enter,
or knowing that a person is climbing over a wall and not stopping them from doing so.
In both of these cases, the guardsmen receive the same punishment as the criminal.
Other articles about guarding imperial palaces, imperial audience halls, and other forbidden places,
all of which have persons in charge of gates and guardsmen,
where they deliberately connive at or are aware of an offense,
follow this article.
ARTICLE: 59.1a-i—All cases of unauthorized entry of the gates of the imperial palace
are punished by two years of penal servitude.
SUBCOMMENTARY:
The imperial palace gates all have name registers (chi-chin 籍禁),
and those who enter without permission to do so
are punished by two years of penal servitude.
Such gates as that of Admirable Virtue are imperial palace gates;
such gates as that of Obedience to Heaven are imperial palace city gates.
Other articles where punishment is required
follow this article on the imperial palace gates.

ARTICLE: 59.1b—Unauthorized entry of the gates of an imperial audience hall is punished by two and one-half years of penal servitude.
59.1c—If the person is carrying a weapon,
the punishment is increased by two degrees in each case.
[2b] SUBCOMMENTARY:
The gates of the Hall of the Supreme Ultimate are examples of such doors.
If the person is carrying a weapon, the punishment is increased two degrees in each case
means that unauthorized entry of the imperial palace gate while carrying a military weapon or a club
is punished by three years of penal servitude.
If the gate is that of an imperial audience hall,
the punishment is life exile at a distance of 2,000 li.
Military weapons

Clubs

Other articles

ARTICLE: 59.2a—Entry into the imperial pavilions

is punished by strangulation.1414Following Shiga Shûzô et al., trs., Yakuchu Nilson ritsuryo (Translations of the Code and the Statutes, hereafter referred to as Translations) vI, 13, n. 1, I translate shang ko 上閤 as imperial pavilion. Shiga states that this term refers to rooms smaller than imperial audience halls that were found near the east and west doors of the Palace of the Supreme Ultimate. The character ko 閣 $should be read ko 閤, here and below, following the KHCPTS edition. See the discussion in des Rotours, Fonctionnaires, II, 630-631.
SUBCOMMENTARY:
In the imperial pavilions
refers to there being imperial pavilions on the east
and west sides of the Hall of the Supreme Ultimate.
There are no name registers at the doors of these halls.
Those who are allowed to enter are listed in an imperial edict.
Those who enter without authorization are punished by strangulation.
Wherever imperial honor guardsmen [52] are stationed
within the imperial pavilions
refers to their not being stationed
but that they enter only when summoned from within.
If a person enters where he should not,
he receives the same punishment as those who enter the gates of an imperial audience hall without authorization,
that is, two and one-half years of penal servitude.
Those who carry weapons are punished by life exile at a distance of 2,000 li.
Imperial palace gates
where there are no name registers
refer to gates such as that of Manifest Respect and Devout Transformation.
Those who go through them,
as well as those who enter improperly and without authorization,
are punished by strangulation.
Where there are imperial honor guardsmen,
the punishment is the same as under the law on unauthorized entry of the gates of an imperial audience hall.
ARTICLE: 59.2b—If a person carrying a weapon enters the imperial presence,

the punishment is decapitation.1515A famous case involving this article concerns the same Ch'ang-sun Wu-chi who headed the commission to revise the Code in A.D. 653. However, since he was the emperor's brother-in-law he was not punished. The case is included in Robert H. van Gulik's T'ang-yin-pi-shih: "Parallel Cases from under the Pear-Tree," pp. 168-169.
[3a] SUBCOMMENTARY:
This refers to carrying weapons into the imperial pavilions as well as entering the gates of the imperial palace.
Even though the person is not carrying a weapon, if he comes into the imperial presence
the punishment is decapitation in both cases.
Through confusion or error
refers to where the unauthorized entry was not intentional.
In such cases a petition may be sent up requesting the imperial decision.
ARTICLE: 59.2d—If a person who is permitted to enter the imperial pavilions
does so carrying even a one-inch knife and there are no imperial honor guardsmen present,
this is also punished as unauthorized entry.
SUBCOMMENTARY:
Permitted to enter the imperial pavilion
refers to being on an imperial edict and, when the imperial honor guard is summoned
to lead the person in,
being allowed to carry such weapons as a sword.
But if the person enters carrying even a one-inch dagger where the imperial honor guard is not present,
the punishment is for unauthorized entry.
If what is carried is not a military weapon or a club,
the punishment is only strangulation.

[4a] QUERY:
For two days or more
an official comes to his office each separate day.
But when the office attendance roll is checked
he is not present.
How can he be punished for not standing duty without a reason
when he did come to the office each day?
But if he is punished for cumulative checks
then the punishment would be heavier than for not standing duty.
If within a ten-day period
the official does come each separate day,
for each absence?
what punishment is to be sentenced
REPLY:
For officials of the eighth rank and below,
when checks of the attendance roll show repeated absences,
each one increases the seriousness of the offense,
and the punishment is for the cumulative number of absences.1111See Article 29,Vol. I, pp. 167 ff.
For those who do not have official rank,
the punishment is administered on the same day and then he is released. 12 12 See Article 498 below.
At first, though the accumulated absences are punished more heavily,
even several will not reach the punishment of penal servitude.
The calculation of days when duty is not stood, even though the punishment is light,
if the number of days is many, then will reach to the punishment of penal servitude.
Therefore if on separate days the official did stand duty, then the punishment follows the absences,
but when he did not come for a whole day, the number of days is calculated.
Sentencing in this way
really carries out the punishment.

QUERY:
If one does not immediately begin mourning upon hearing of a death
but rather begins on some other selected day,
what is the punishment if the offense is discovered after one has begun mourning?
REPLY:
According to the Book of Rites,
"When one is wearing mourning for relatives of the first degree of mourning, the voice in lamenting
seems to continue (until it fades away) and not to return.
For relatives of the second degree of mourning, the voice
seems to come and go.
For relatives of the third degree of mourning,
after three changes of pitch, the sound is extended and then dies away.
For relatives of the fourth and fifth degree of mourning,
it is sufficient that the sound express sorrow."1717 Li-chi, "chien-chuan," p. 955; Couvreur, Li ki, II, 570.
According to the rules of rites,
there are different levels of seriousness.
The learning of death is common to all,
but the feelings are different.
For relatives within the second degree of mourning
if one does not immediately begin mourning,
even though one does so on a later day,
there must be punishment.
So for such relatives the punishment is the heavier following the law 18 on doing what ought not to be done. 18The blank here should read fa 法, following the SPTK edition.
For relatives of the third degree of mourning,

the punishment is the lighter for doing what ought not to be done. 19 19 See Article 450 below.The heavier punishment is eighty blows with the heavy stick, and the lighter punishment forty blows with the light stick.
For relatives of the fourth degree of mourning or less,
it is sufficient that the sound of their mourning express sorrow.
Thus they should not be punished.
But if the offense is discovered before they have begun mourning,
they should be punished for not having begun mourning.

If there is an unauthorized increase in taxes that goes to the government [7b] of goods worth more than a full one [118] hundred p'i of silk,
which the law would collect from a group of persons,
then the punishment is for one-half of the value of the goods.
One-half of the value being fifty p'i of silk,
the punishment is for illicit goods obtained through malfeasance
where the maximum punishment is three years of penal servitude.
If the illicit goods go to a private person,
the punishment is for subverting the law.
Reference to going to a private person
does not require that the goods go to the person himself,
but that they not go to the government.
Thus if the private person is a salaried official, 48 48 That is, a ranked official. On their salaries, see Niida, Statutes, p. 321.
for subverting the law, illicit goods worth one p'i of silk are punished by one hundred blows with the heavy stick,
increased one degree for goods worth each further p'i of silk.
The punishment for fifteen ch'ih is strangulation.
The punishment for those officials who have no salary is reduced one degree
so that the punishment for twenty p'i is strangulation.

Now 49 it is stated: "Where punishment reaches the death penalty , life exile with added labor is substituted." 49 Shiga, Translations, vi, 262, says that ling 令, "statute," is an error for chin , "now," though without being able to cite any edition that reads this way. It is likely that he is right since (1) the quote does not occur in the statutes, and (2) the characters are sufficiently alike that such a mistake could be easily made.
So in neither case is the criminal punished by strangulation.
Of the taxes collected, if some goes to the government
and some to private persons,
then the punishments are not the same
and it is proper that the punishment should be for the combined amount.
So if of the taxes that have been collected without authorization are worth one hundred p'i,
ninety going to the government
and ten to a private person,
of the goods worth ninety p'i of silk that went to the government, one-half is forty-five p'i,
which is punished by two and one-half years of penal servitude.
Halving the ten p'i that went to a private person
is also punished by two and one-half years of penal servitude.
These may not be combined to make five years.
Rather, the goods worth ten p'i of silk that went to the private person are combined with the goods worth ninety p'i of silk that went to the government
to make one hundred p'i.
One half of this is fifty p'i,
for which the punishment is three years of penal servitude.

[121] QUERY:
Suppose a person makes the wife a ying concubine
or a ying concubine the wife,
or makes a concubine a ying concubine
or a ying concubine the concubine.

What is the punishment?5959Ying concubines were of higher status than ordinary concubines. During the T'ang period, only officials of the fifth rank and above could have such women. See Vol. 1, pp. 82, 83, and 83, n. 194.
REPLY:
According to the Articles on Assaults and Accusations,
"If a ying concubine commits a crime against her husband's wife,
the punishment is one degree less than for a concubine.
If a concubine commits a crime against a ying concubine, the punishment is increased one degree above that for a person of non-kin status."
[The Commentary states:] " In other articles where there is no provision about ying concubines,
they are treated the same as concubines."60 60 See Article 326 below.
Thus if a husband commits a crime against a ying concubine,
it is treated the same as if she were a concubine.
The question, then, is not whether the wife, [11a] a ying concubine, or a concubine have committed offenses against each other,
but whether the article increases or decreases the punishment for such offenses.
If the husband commits an offense against a ying concubine,
the article considers it as having been against a concubine.
If the wife is made a ying concubine,
the punishment is the same as if the wife is made a concubine.
If a ying concubine is made the wife,
the punishment is also the same as if a concubine is made the wife.
If a ying concubine is made a concubine,
neither the Code nor the Statutes has a provision for this,
so it is proper that punishment be the heavier for doing what ought not to be done,
that is, eighty blows with the heavy stick.6161 See Article 450 below.
If a concubine is made a ying concubine,
the Statutes have a ruling, 62 62 Unfortunately we do not know what this ruling was. See Niida, Statutes, p. 251.
but the Code does not.
So the punishment can only be that for violating a statute.6363 See Article 449 below. The punishment is fifty blows with the light stick.
If these changes in status are due
to a certificate of appointment being given to the person who made them,

the law on falsely giving a person an office is followed.6464 See Article 370 below. The reason for the change in the certificate of appointment is that only officials of the fifth rank and above could have ying concubines. Still, the punishment is very severe, being life exile at a distance of 2,000 li.
If a concubine is fraudulently made a ying concubine and falsely assumes the surname and name of a ying concubine,
and only then does the person get the certificate of appointment,
following the law
on a person's falsely adding to his merits
in order to get an office.6565This is the third part of Article 370.
the punishment is one year of penal servitude
